input.idea: Why I started building TikMaker. There was chaos in my head: it’s hard to understand how to analyse successful videos, it takes a lot of time and some kind of structure. I wanted my videos to have one brand and one library, all videos easy to edit by hand, a place to write the script, and AI helping me there. I also wanted to learn to build AI agents, so I thought the most useful place is to put one right inside TikMaker. So it’s a personal video, but it also shows what TikMaker is.

template.reason: This template is a perfect match because it explicitly fits a creator telling why they built their own tool starting from the specific chaos and pain they faced.

hooks.text: Everyone's using AI video tools like a messy puzzle.
Why I stopped the chaos and started building TikMaker.
Everyone's using AI to make videos, but organizing them is painful.

hook.text: Analysing viral TikToks broke my brain. So I built TikMaker

prompt.system:
You are the producer of a short-video channel (TikTok, Reels, Shorts).
Your job in this step: choose how the video will be told, by picking ONE template
from the list you are given. You do not write the video yet.

You get the channel, the video idea and the templates.
Pick the template whose "when to use" fits the idea best; the length matters less.
A template's "needs" are the facts its required scenes are built on. Pick one the idea
can fill with its OWN facts: a rise-to-success story needs a success to show, a how-to
needs steps, a list needs items. If the idea lacks what a template needs, that template
does not fit, however close its topic is.
Never invent a template: answer only with an id from the list.
score: 5 = made for this idea and the idea has every fact it needs, 3 = workable,
1 = nothing in the list fits.
reason: one or two sentences for the creator, in plain English, about this idea.
prompt.user:
Channel: TikMaker and AI coding. Mostly TikMaker itself: what it can do, how a video gets made with it, new features and how it is being built with AI (build in public). Audience: Creators who want to make short videos faster with AI, and developers or beginners who build apps with AI and want to work faster without breaking things.

Templates:
- id: analogy-explainer
  name: Explained with characters
  what: A concept explained through a small invented world or everyday analogy
  when to use: An idea that is an abstract concept (economics, health, finance) that becomes clear as a story.
  needs: problem, step, concept-term, real-case, lesson
  length: 26–63 s
- id: app-list
  name: Free apps list
  what: A quick list of apps, one per scene, each shown on screen
  when to use: An idea that recommends several apps or tools for one device or audience.
  needs: app-count, device-or-audience, app-name, app-feature
  length: 14–62 s
- id: brand-origin
  name: Rise of a brand
  what: From a humble start, through hardship, to a big brand
  when to use: An idea that is the history of a brand, product or founder that has already grown big: the idea gives the success to show (users, money, years). Not a creator telling why they built their own tool.
  needs: year-or-result, brand, founder, start, hardship, time-jump, result-number
  length: 43–80 s
- id: build-it-fast
  name: Build it fast
  what: Show the finished thing, then every step that built it
  when to use: An idea where the viewer can build something real in minutes with a tool.
  needs: result, time, tool-name, step, screen-recording
  length: 20–51 s
- id: dark-true-story
  name: Creepy true story
  what: A dark or strange true story told step by step to a shocking ending
  when to use: An idea that is a real crime, legend or eerie event.
  needs: place-or-person, event, ending
  length: 15–51 s
- id: explained-in-time
  name: Explained in 60 seconds
  what: A complex topic explained in a promised short time, often to an unlikely audience
  when to use: An idea that is a complex topic the viewer finds hard and wants explained quickly.
  needs: nothing special
  length: 35–54 s
- id: how-to-steps
  name: How-to steps
  what: A how-to promise followed by numbered steps on screen
  when to use: An idea that is a concrete task the viewer wants to do with a tool, in a few steps.
  needs: task, tool-name
  length: 32–43 s
- id: myth-vs-reality
  name: Myth vs reality
  what: What people think, then how it really works, with the proof
  when to use: An idea that corrects a common belief or reveals a hidden side of something familiar.
  needs: belief, background, reality, step, twist
  length: 26–59 s
- id: new-tool-news
  name: New tool news
  what: A just-released free tool, its benefits, a quick demo and a comment-keyword offer
  when to use: An idea that is news about a newly released or newly free tool.
  needs: who-released, tool-name, benefit, keyword, resource
  length: 30–107 s
- id: pain-to-fix
  name: Problem then fix
  what: The broken or painful way first, then the tool that fixes it, shown working
  when to use: An idea where a tool fixes a pain the audience recognises, including a creator telling why they built their own tool: the pain they had, then the tool that fixes it.
  needs: pain, task, screen-recording
  length: 30–40 s
- id: plot-recap
  name: Story recap
  what: A plot, journey or character backstory retold event by event
  when to use: An idea that recaps an episode, myth, game lore or a character's story.
  needs: story-name, setting, ending
  length: 48–181 s
- id: product-promo
  name: Product promo
  what: A product's benefits shown one by one through its interface, ending on where to get it
  when to use: An idea that promotes one product or service.
  needs: product-name
  length: 11–30 s
- id: question-answered
  name: Big question answered
  what: A why or how question, answered step by step with diagrams
  when to use: An idea that is a question the audience has wondered about.
  needs: question
  length: 43–71 s
- id: ranked-countdown
  name: Top N countdown
  what: Ranked items counted down to number one
  when to use: An idea that ranks a set of things by some measure.
  needs: rank-count, ranked-thing, rank-number, item-name, item-detail
  length: 25–60 s
- id: rapid-facts
  name: Rapid-fire facts
  what: Many short facts in a row, one per scene, with the strongest kept for last
  when to use: An idea that is a collection of short surprising facts around one theme.
  needs: theme, fact
  length: 40–56 s
- id: single-fact
  name: One surprising fact
  what: One fact built up line by line to a short reveal
  when to use: An idea that is a single surprising or eerie fact that fits in under 20 seconds.
  needs: topic
  length: 7–16 s
- id: software-tutorial
  name: Software how-to
  what: A finished result first, then the steps to make it in the software
  when to use: An idea that is a specific thing to make in a common program (PowerPoint, GitHub, a no-code tool).
  needs: result, software
  length: 14–53 s
- id: tool-deep-dive
  name: Tool explained
  what: What a tool is, how it differs, and what it really does
  when to use: An idea that explains one popular tool or model and how to think about it.
  needs: tool-name, difference, main-point
  length: 49–78 s
- id: tool-spotlight
  name: Tool spotlight
  what: One website or tool shown working, often as a numbered series part
  when to use: An idea that is a single useful website, repo or tool the viewer probably has not seen.
  needs: tool-category, series-part, screen-recording
  length: 10–56 s
- id: tool-tips-keyword
  name: Tool tips list
  what: Numbered tips for one tool, each named and then shown working, ending with a comment-keyword offer
  when to use: An idea that is a handful of concrete tips, skills or add-ons for one tool the audience already uses.
  needs: tool-name, tip-count, tip-number, tip-name, keyword, resource
  length: 47–88 s

prompt.system:
You write the opening line (hook) of a short vertical video (TikTok, Reels, Shorts):
the words shown and spoken in the first two seconds, which decide whether people keep watching.

Write THREE different hooks for the idea.
At least two must follow a formula from the list: fill the formula in for this idea,
do not copy its example. formulaId = that formula's id, or null for a hook of your own.
Fill a formula only with what the idea says: never claim something it does not
(no "I switched from…", no number, no result the idea does not give).
Each hook: one line, at most 12 words, plain spoken English, no hashtags, no emojis.
score: 5 = people stop scrolling, 3 = fine, 1 = weak.

Formulas:
- id: everyone-uses-it-wrong
  type: pain-shown
  formula: Everyone's using [tool] like [wrong analogy].
  example: Everyone's using Claude Code like it's a magic wand.
- id: in-year-subject-did
  type: story
  formula: In [year or era], [subject] [did something].
  example: In 1946, four brothers named Kashio
- id: saw-someone-doing-it-like-this
  type: pain-shown
  formula: Saw [someone] [doing a task] like this
  example: Saw the intern visualizing his data like this
- id: everyone-uses-but
  type: contrarian
  formula: Everyone's using [trending tool] to [goal], but [pain].
  example: Everyone's using Claude Code to build AI agents
- id: characters-live-in-two-places
  type: story
  formula: [Characters] live in two [places]: [A] and [B].
  example: Gorillas live in two countries
- id: did-you-know-spooky-place
  type: story
  formula: Did you know that in [spooky place]...
  example: Did you know that in an old house on the outskirts of Hiroshima...
- id: dramatic-quote
  type: story
  formula: "[The most dramatic line spoken in the story]"
  example: Why did you kill my wife and daughter ?
- id: i-switched-from
  type: story
  formula: I switched from [tool A] to [tool B].
  example: I switched from Cursor to Claude Code.
- id: everyone-without-is-wasting
  type: contrarian
  formula: Everyone using [tool] without [feature] is just wasting their [resource].
  example: Everyone using Claude without skills is just wasting their tokens.
- id: you-are-the-only
  type: contrarian
  formula: You are the only [statement that sounds impossible].
  example: You are the only person alive.
- id: you-might-think
  type: contrarian
  formula: When you [everyday action], you might think [misconception]...
  example: When you visit a website, you might think that your computer is connecting with
- id: characters-on-a-job
  type: story
  formula: Alright guys, we've got a [job] to do. Where's the [problem] this time?
  example: Alright guys, we've got a job to do. Where's the pain this time?
- id: imagine-you-have
  type: story
  formula: Imagine you have [valuable thing] in your [place].
  example: Imagine you have ten thousand dollars

prompt.system:
You write the script of a short vertical video (TikTok, Reels, Shorts).

Tell ONE connected story. The idea may be written as loose thoughts in any order: sort
them into the order the template's scenes tell (the problem before the fix, the cause
before the result), and let every scene follow from the one before it – the voiceovers
read in a row must make sense as one spoken text. A scene that promises something ("what I learned", "here's why") is
followed by the scene that says it.

Follow the template's scenes in their order. A "repeatable" scene may appear several
times in a row (one per step or item); an "optional" scene may be left out – then put it
in "skipped" with a short reason. Never use a role the template does not have.
A scene's "facts" come from the idea only – never invent a tool, a number or a result.
When the idea has no fact for a scene, leave it out if it is optional; if it is required,
fill it with what the idea does say rather than with an invented claim.
Its "creative" parts are yours to word.

The first scene is the hook: say the chosen hook as it is, and show its key words.
Link each scene to the next the way the template says ("→ next"), using the
transition phrases for that link. End with a call to action that follows one of the
CTA formulas, unless the template's CTA types include "none" and none fits.
The call to action never sends people to a link, a website, a download or a giveaway
the idea does not mention – then pick a CTA formula that needs none of those.

For every scene:
- voiceover: what is said, natural spoken English
- onScreen: the key words shown big, not the whole sentence
- visual: what the viewer sees, concrete (a terminal running a command, a settings page,
  an app icon), never "something engaging"
- needsRecording: true when the scene shows real actions in an app (clicks, menus,
  several windows) or a real result only a recording can prove; false for a single
  command, a line of code, a key press or a simple graphic – the video editor draws
  those.

Keep within the limits. Each scene lasts about as long as its voiceover: fill the wanted
length – add more steps or items with the repeatable scenes, keep the optional scenes
that help – rather than stopping short.

Template: Problem then fix – The broken or painful way first, then the tool that fixes it, shown working
Scenes:
- opening / hook (2–2.8 s): Shows or states the wrong way people do it. [required] → next: contrast; facts: pain; creative: who
- build / setup (2.4–4 s): Sets the scene of the task. [required] → next: sequence; facts: task
- build / problem (3–7 s): Names what goes wrong. [optional] [repeatable] → next: open-loop-payoff; facts: problem
- core / reveal (2.2–4.6 s): Names the fix. [optional] [repeatable] → next: sequence; facts: tool-name
- core / demo (3–7 s): Shows the fix working on screen. [required] [repeatable] → next: sequence; facts: screen-recording
- climax / benefit (3.4–6.6 s): States what changed. [optional] → next: bridge; facts: gain
- close / cta (3–3 s): Points to the full guide. [optional] → next: none; facts: resource

Transition phrases:
- sequence: First, | Second, | Third, | First is | Second is | Third is
- contrast: But | Instead | Instead of just | But instead, | but in reality, | but that's not how
- bridge: So if you want | So just | To get the full | For a PDF | So want to try it for yourself? | Now you might be wondering...
- open-loop-payoff: It's called | You have probably heard of | Here's the easiest way | All roads lead to Rome... | And that's why... | Anthropic just dropped

CTA formulas (types allowed: none):
- none: end on the last scene, without a call to action (skip the cta scene)

Limits, from the analysis of successful videos:
- speak at most 3.4 words per second
- a scene lasts at most 9 s, the hook at most 5 s
- at most 15 words on screen in a scene

prompt.system:
You lay out the scenes of a short vertical video (TikTok, Reels, Shorts).
Every layout example is taken from a successful video. For every scene, pick ONE
example from that scene's list (layoutExampleId) and fill each of its pictures, in
the order they are listed (fills):
- a logo picture: an id from Logos
- a prop picture: an id from Props
- any other picture (a recording, a screen, a photo, a phone): one short sentence
  telling the user what to record or capture there for this scene.
Pick the example whose arrangement suits what the scene shows; when a scene is
marked "own recording: yes", prefer an example with a recording or screen.
Answer with one entry per scene, in the same order.
prompt.user:
Channel: TikMaker and AI coding. Mostly TikMaker itself: what it can do, how a video gets made with it, new features and how it is being built with AI (build in public). Around that, short concrete videos about other AI tools, vibe coding and Claude Code: one problem or one feature per video, shown on screen rather than told.
Idea: Why I started building TikMaker. There was chaos in my head: it’s hard to understand how to analyse successful videos, it takes a lot of time and some kind of structure. I wanted my videos to have one brand and one library, all videos easy to edit by hand, a place to write the script, and AI helping me there. I also wanted to learn to build AI agents, so I thought the most useful place is to put one right inside TikMaker. So it’s a personal video, but it also shows what TikMaker is.

Logos: bolt, chatgpt, claude, claude-ai-symbol, claude-svg, cloudflare, discord, elevenlabs, figma, gemini, github, gmail, google-chrome, grok, kilo-code, lovable, midjourney, netlify, reddit, remotion, remotion, stripe, supabase, vercel, vs-code, x
Props: broken-glass, broom, browser-window, bug, card-declined, clock, coin, credit-card, database, document, dollar-cupure, envelope, eye, frustration, fuel-gauge, idea, key, layer-stack, link, padlock, paper-documents, pen, pin, plane, pricetag, puzzle-joined, puzzle-piece, question, robot-helpers, screen-panel, shop, sync-arrows, target, tower-leaning, two-users, user-avatar, uturn, wallet

Scene 1 (hook) – own recording: no
  On screen: Analysing viral TikToks broke my brain
  Shows: A messy folder of random TikTok downloads on a computer desktop
  Examples:
  - hook-02: pictures: 1 image → a sentence: what to capture; with text. The background carries the frame: a striking full-frame illustration of the subject. The hook is split around a huge title: small line above, title in the middle, small line below, all centred.
  - hook-04: pictures: 1 recording → a sentence: what to capture; 2 logo → a logo id; 3 logo → a logo id; 4 logo → a logo id; with text. Result on top, how it was made below. The tool logos zigzag left, right, left at different sizes instead of sitting in a row, which keeps the lower half lively; they are the list the video will go through.
  - hook-05: pictures: 1 screen → a sentence: what to capture; with text. A silent visual hook: no captions, no headline over the frame. The opening animation (the laptop opening, the screen lighting up) is the hook; the dark vignette puts all the light on the screen.
  - hook-07: pictures: 1 image → a sentence: what to capture; with text. Topic on top, a funny picture in the middle, the twist below: the same sandwich as hook-02 but light and playful. A serious topic plus a silly promise ('explained by ducks') is the curiosity gap. Plain white background, nothing else.
  - hook-08: pictures: 1 image → a sentence: what to capture; 2 image → a sentence: what to capture; with text. How to use landscape material in 9:16: the sharp photo across the middle, and behind it the same photo zoomed to fill the frame and heavily blurred, so there are no black bars and the colours match. A meme character adds the emotion; the quote is the hook.

Scene 2 (setup) – own recording: no
  On screen: Total chaos in my head
  Shows: Notes app open with scattered, unstructured thoughts about viral videos
  Examples:
  - setup-01: pictures: 1 screen → a sentence: what to capture; no text. No separate text: the prompt inside the screen is the text. Zooming in instead of cutting keeps it one continuous object and points at what to read.
  - setup-03: pictures: 1 image → a sentence: what to capture; no text. Storytelling format: the voiceover tells the story, every beat gets its own picture with a slow Ken Burns move, and the only text is the captions, one big word at a time in the centre (white, bold italic, dark shadow). No headlines, no layout to read: the picture and the voice carry it.

Scene 3 (problem) – own recording: no
  On screen: No structure, takes too much time
  Shows: A blank script document with a blinking cursor
  Examples:
  - problem-01: pictures: 1 logo → a logo id; 2 image → a sentence: what to capture; with text. The problem shown as damage: the sentence names the pain, the thing it costs appears as a solid plate and then cracks. Light grey background with a dotted-grid patch behind the plate, channel watermark at about y 86.

Scene 4 (reveal) – own recording: yes
  On screen: Built TikMaker
  Shows: The TikMaker app dashboard opening up on screen
  Examples:
  - reveal-01: pictures: 1 browser → a sentence: what to capture; no text. Shows WHERE to go. Cropping the browser lets the tab and address bar fill the frame instead of a small whole window. A colourful, blurred desktop wallpaper behind it says 'this is a real computer' and stands apart from the dark site.
  - reveal-02: pictures: 1 logo → a logo id; 2 image → a sentence: what to capture; 3 phone → a sentence: what to capture; with text. The product revealed as a stack, top to bottom: icon, name, where to get it, what it looks like. Captions sit very low here; in TikMaker keep them above the bottom safe margin.

Scene 5 (demo) – own recording: yes
  On screen: One brand and one library
  Shows: The library view in TikMaker showing organized video projects
  Examples:
  - demo-01: pictures: 1 recording → a sentence: what to capture; no text. One big thing to look at: the screen being demonstrated fills most of the frame. Captions sit inside its lower part and stay at the same height for the rest of the video; only the hook had them higher.
  - demo-02: pictures: 1 prop → a prop id; with text. Shows the action as input → working: what you type on top, the tool thinking in the middle. Nothing is shown before it is needed.
  - demo-04: pictures: 1 screen → a sentence: what to capture; no text. The app shown whole, as a tidy card, on a playful background (muted blue with thin hand-drawn lines and a few small yellow stars), so the screenshot does not look like a bare screen grab.
  - demo-05: pictures: 1 browser → a sentence: what to capture; no text. How you use it: the input step. Zooming the browser past the frame's sides makes the prompt readable on a phone; a blurred colourful wallpaper shows above and below.

Scene 6 (demo) – own recording: yes
  On screen: AI helps write scripts
  Shows: Typing a script in TikMaker with an AI assistant panel active on the side
  Examples:
  - demo-01: pictures: 1 recording → a sentence: what to capture; no text. One big thing to look at: the screen being demonstrated fills most of the frame. Captions sit inside its lower part and stay at the same height for the rest of the video; only the hook had them higher.
  - demo-02: pictures: 1 prop → a prop id; with text. Shows the action as input → working: what you type on top, the tool thinking in the middle. Nothing is shown before it is needed.
  - demo-04: pictures: 1 screen → a sentence: what to capture; no text. The app shown whole, as a tidy card, on a playful background (muted blue with thin hand-drawn lines and a few small yellow stars), so the screenshot does not look like a bare screen grab.
  - demo-05: pictures: 1 browser → a sentence: what to capture; no text. How you use it: the input step. Zooming the browser past the frame's sides makes the prompt readable on a phone; a blurred colourful wallpaper shows above and below.

Scene 7 (benefit) – own recording: yes
  On screen: AI agent inside TikMaker
  Shows: The AI agent chat interface responding inside the app
  Examples:
  - benefit-01: pictures: 1 phone → a sentence: what to capture; 2 logo → a logo id; with text. One benefit = one word next to one screen: phone left, word right, the two balanced across the middle. The purple shapes move between corners from frame to frame.
  - benefit-02: pictures: 1 logo → a logo id; 2 image → a sentence: what to capture; 3 phone → a sentence: what to capture; with text. Logo, heading, then a phone in front of a moving row of examples: shows variety without clutter. Plain white background so the colourful cards carry the frame.
  - benefit-04: pictures: 1 recording → a sentence: what to capture; with text. Benefit stated on top of the action that delivers it: the full-frame zoomed recording shows the change, one yellow text box says what you gain. The box sits low, over rows that do not matter, so the important part of the screen stays clear.
